title: The Divine Liturgy
hookLine: the Orthodox service, much of it from Chrysostom's time, sung start to finish

lines: A DEACON CARRIES THE GOSPEL BOOK.
cards: Smoke from a censer, drifting up past painted faces of saints. Candles everywhere. Hardly any pews; people stand.
A choir you can't quite see holds one long chord. Then a deacon comes out through a door in the icon screen, carrying a heavy gold-covered book held high.
Before the readings he sings out a short call, loud enough to wake anyone drifting off: Wisdom! Let us attend! Everyone straightens.
This is the Divine Liturgy, the Sunday service of Orthodox Christians, and nearly all of it is sung.

teach.b: First, the name. Liturgy is the church's word for worship offered together. Divine, because Orthodox Christians understand it as heaven's worship, joined for a while on earth.
The service used most Sundays carries the name of Saint John Chrysostom, a preacher of the early church; tradition credits him with shaping it. Second, it's sung.
Nearly every line is chanted or sung, by priest, deacon, choir and people, back and forth.
The deacon calls out a petition, for peace, for the sick, for travelers, and the people answer each one: Lord, have mercy. The answer stays the same while the needs change. Third, the movement.

Twice the clergy come out in procession: first with the gospel book, the little entrance; later with the bread and wine, the great entrance, while the choir sings the Cherubic Hymn, which asks the people to lay aside all earthly cares.

teach.h: TWO ENTRANCES, AND THE SERAPHIM'S SONG.
teach.b: Then, as the bread and wine are offered, the people sing a hymn built on the song the prophet Isaiah heard the seraphim singing: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory."
Orthodox Christians speak of the liturgy as joining the angels' worship. Fourth, the call.

teach.h: LET US ATTEND, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: Again and again the deacon says it: Wisdom, let us attend. Before the readings, before the creed, before the gifts. It isn't decoration.
It's a wake-up call for a mind that wanders, sung over and over, because minds wander over and over.

how: Orthodox Christians gather on Sundays for the Divine Liturgy, usually the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, which is chanted or sung throughout; worshipers often stand, light candles, venerate icons and receive communion at the end.

games.q: you're the deacon. the readings are about to begin, and half the room has drifted off into their own thoughts. what do you do?
o: sing out: wisdom! let us attend!
games.why: the deacon calls them back with a short call, sung. the liturgy expects minds to wander, and calls them back again and again.

practice: If you can, play a recording of the Divine Liturgy, or any old church music sung by voices, quietly; if not, listen to the room around you.
Don't try to follow the words; each time your mind wanders, don't scold it, just say inside, let us attend, and come back to the sound. If you pray, you can join the old answer: Lord, have mercy.

wordCard.voice: The Divine Liturgy. The Sunday service of Orthodox Christians, sung nearly from start to finish, which carries the name of John Chrysostom and comes to the table near its end.

orig.note: Greek: let us attend, let us pay attention — the deacon's call before the readings in the Divine Liturgy.

carryVoice: Your line: let us attend. Sung by a deacon, kept by anyone. See you tomorrow.
